chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: rectangles first, then triangles as half rectangles, then every other shape cut into rectangles and triangles. Each formula is earned by a cut and a rearrange before it is used, and each is checked on a figure the student can count.

points.title: Predict, then check
points.text: Each idea opens with a guess: which rectangle needs more powder, which triangle is bigger, will the area change when the shape slides. The video or the interactive step then checks the guess.

points.title: Cut and rearrange
points.text: Dissection is the engine of the chapter. A parallelogram, a rhombus and a trapezium are each cut and moved into a rectangle or parallelogram of the same area before any formula is written.

points.title: Height is perpendicular
points.text: Every formula uses a height that meets the base at a right angle, never a slanting side. Obtuse triangles and slanting trapeziums are handled by subtracting or adding pieces.

points.title: Tools only where the moving is the idea
points.text: Four interactive tools, each used once: stretching rectangles, sliding a triangle's top vertex, cutting a parallelogram and joining two trapeziums. Other topics are taught by worked examples.

modules.module_summary: Area counts unit squares, so a rectangle is length times width and perimeter cannot stand in for area. A triangle is half of a rectangle on the same base and height, and that one formula finds altitudes, splits shapes into equal parts and explains triangles between parallel lines.

concepts.concept_name: How many ways to cut a square into 4 equal areas?

content.text:
7.1 Rectangle and Squares
How many different ways can you divide a square into 4 parts of equal area?
One can actually think of infinitely many such ways! Consider a division, such as, and alter each part as follows.
In each part, the area is compressed along one edge and expanded along another edge. If both the compression and expansion are of the same magnitude, then all 4 parts still have the same area!
Try to think of different creative ways to divide a square into 4 parts of equal area.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many ways can a square be cut into 4 parts of equal area? Two? Five? More?
2. Four small squares is one way. Push a notch into one edge of each part and push the same bump out of another edge: the shapes change, the areas do not.
3. Since every notch can be a different shape, there are infinitely many ways. Equal area does not mean equal shape. So what exactly is area, and how do we measure it?

content.text:
You might have seen the rangoli art form, in which regions of different shapes are beautifully coloured using rangoli powder.
Which of these rectangles requires more rangoli powder to be coloured, if the colouring is done evenly?
Clearly, the rectangle having sidelengths 7 cm and 4 cm contains 7 × 4 = 28 unit squares, and the rectangle having sidelengths 8 cm and 3 cm contains 8 × 3 = 24 unit squares.
Area of a rectangle = length × width.
The areas of the rectangles as seen in the previous problem are generally written as 28 sq. cm and 24 sq. cm, or as 28 cm² and 24 cm².

content.text:
Worked example: A rangoli artist has a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle and an 8 cm by 3 cm rectangle. Which needs more powder?
1. Count unit squares in the first: 7 × 4 = 28.
2. Count unit squares in the second: 8 × 3 = 24.
3. 28 is more than 24.
Answer: The 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle needs more powder: 28 cm² against 24 cm²

content.text:
What is the area of each triangle in this rectangle?
We have seen that the diagonal of a rectangle divides it into two congruent triangles. So, the area of each triangle is half the area of the rectangle.
In terms of unit squares, half the area fills exactly half the number of unit squares.
So the area of each triangle is 1/2 × 7 × 4 = 14 cm².

content.text:
Why do we count the number of unit squares to assign measures for area? Couldn't we have just used the perimeter of a region, i.e., the length of its boundary as a measure of its area?
If two regions have the same perimeter, can't we conclude that they have the same area? Or, if one region has a larger perimeter than another region, can't we conclude that it also has a larger area?
The perimeter of a region is not indicative of its area. The reason is that regions can have the same perimeter but different areas, and vice versa.
Perimeter of Region 1 > Perimeter of Region 2, but Area of Region 1 < Area of Region 2.
Find two rectangles that are examples of such regions. If needed, use a grid paper for this.

content.text:
Worked example: Compare a 10 cm by 1 cm strip with a 5 cm by 4 cm rectangle: perimeter and area.
1. Strip perimeter: 2 × (10 + 1) = 22 cm. Strip area: 10 × 1 = 10 cm².
2. Rectangle perimeter: 2 × (5 + 4) = 18 cm. Rectangle area: 5 × 4 = 20 cm².
3. 22 > 18 but 10 < 20.
Answer: The strip has the larger perimeter (22 cm) but the smaller area (10 cm²)

content.text:
Worked example: Compare a 4 by 4 square with a thin zigzag made of 9 unit squares joined edge to edge in one line with bends.
1. Square: perimeter 4 × 4 = 16 units, area 16 square units.
2. Zigzag: each square shares edges with its neighbours, leaving 2 × 9 + 2 = 20 unit edges on the boundary, so perimeter 20 units.
3. Zigzag area: 9 square units.
Answer: The zigzag has the larger perimeter (20 units against 16) but the smaller area (9 against 16)

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 1): Identify the missing sidelengths. (i) A plus shaped figure is made of four rectangles: a 28 in² piece whose right edge rises 4 in above a 21 in² piece of length 7 in, a 35 in² piece of width 3 in plus the width of the 28 in² piece, and a 14 in² strip that hangs 2 in below the 35 in² piece; find the width of the 14 in² strip. (ii) A 29 m² piece and an 11 m² piece are both 4 m tall, and the bold rectangle made of the 29 m² piece and the piece below it has area 50 m²; find the missing sides.
1. (i) The 21 in² piece is 7 in long, so its height is 21 ÷ 7 = 3 in.
2. The 28 in² piece is 4 + 3 = 7 in tall, so its width is 28 ÷ 7 = 4 in.
3. The 35 in² piece is 3 + 4 = 7 in wide, so its height is 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in.
4. The 14 in² strip is 5 + 2 = 7 in tall, so its width is 14 ÷ 7 = 2 in.
5. (ii) Top widths: 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 m and 11 ÷ 4 = 2.75 m.
6. The lower piece has area 50 − 29 = 21 m² and width 7.25 m, so its height is 21 ÷ 7.25 ≈ 2.9 m.
Answer: (i) 2 in, with 3 in, 4 in and 5 in on the way. (ii) 7.25 m and 2.75 m across the top, and a lower height of 84/29 m, about 2.9 m

2. The 28 in² piece is 4 + 3 = 7 in tall, so its width is 28 ÷ 7 = 4 in.
3. The 35 in² piece is 3 + 4 = 7 in wide, so its height is 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in.
4. The 14 in² strip is 5 + 2 = 7 in tall, so its width is 14 ÷ 7 = 2 in.

6. The lower piece has area 50 − 29 = 21 m² and width 7.25 m, so its height is 21 ÷ 7.25 ≈ 2.9 m.

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 2): A path (the shaded portion) is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a rectangle ABCD. (i) What measurements do you need to find the area of the path? Assign values and give a formula. (ii) If the width of the path along each side is given, can you find its area? If not, what else do you need? (iii) Does the area of the path change when the outer rectangle is moved while keeping the park inside it?
1. (i) Measure the length and width of ABCD and of EFGH.
2. Area of path = area of ABCD − area of EFGH. With ABCD 20 m by 14 m and EFGH 16 m by 10 m: 20 × 14 − 16 × 10 = 280 − 160 = 120 m².
3. (ii) The widths alone are not enough; we also need the park's length and width. With a park 16 m by 10 m and widths 2 m on every side, break the path into two long strips 20 m by 2 m and two short strips 10 m by 2 m: 2 × 40 + 2 × 20 = 120 m².
4. (iii) Moving ABCD around the park changes the widths but not the two rectangles, so the path area stays the same.
Answer: (i) Path area = area of ABCD − area of EFGH (120 m² for the chosen values). (ii) Also need the park's sides; same 120 m². (iii) No, the area does not change

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 3): A plot has sides 14 m and 12 m with a crosspath. What other measurements do you need to find the area of the crosspath? Assign values and give a formula.
1. We need the widths of the two paths: p for the path along the 14 m side and q for the path along the 12 m side.
2. The two strips are 14 × p and 12 × q, but they overlap in a p by q square counted twice.
3. Area = 14p + 12q − pq. With p = 1 m and q = 2 m: 14 × 1 + 12 × 2 − 1 × 2 = 14 + 24 − 2 = 36 m².
Answer: The widths of the two paths; area = 14p + 12q − pq, which is 36 m² when the widths are 1 m and 2 m

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 4): Find the area of the spiral tube shown in the figure. The tube has the same width (1 unit) throughout, and its straight parts measure 20, 20, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, 5 and 5 along the outside.
1. The hint: an L shaped tube with arms 5 and 5 has the same area as a straight tube of length 5 + 5 − 1 = 9, because the corner square is counted in both arms.
2. Add all the straight lengths: 20 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 120.
3. There are 8 bends, each counted twice, so subtract 8: 120 − 8 = 112.
4. The straightened tube is 112 units long and 1 unit wide: 112 × 1 = 112.
Answer: 112 square units

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5): A square is divided into regions 1, 2 and 3. If the sidelength of the square is doubled, what is the increase in the areas of the regions 1, 2 and 3? Give reasons.
1. Doubling the side doubles every length in the figure, both across and up.
2. Each region's area is multiplied by 2 × 2 = 4.
3. So each region grows by 4 − 1 = 3 times its old area.
Answer: Each region becomes 4 times as big, an increase of 3 times its original area

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 6): Divide a square into 4 parts by drawing two perpendicular lines inside the square, then rearrange the pieces to get a larger square with a hole inside.
1. Draw two perpendicular lines through the square that are not parallel to its sides; the 4 pieces are congruent.
2. Turn the pieces so that each right angle points outward and the long edges run round the outside.
3. The outside forms a bigger square; the gap in the middle is a small square hole.
4. The area of the big square minus the hole equals the area of the original square.
Answer: The 4 congruent pieces form a larger square around a square hole; total area is unchanged

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students compare two rectangles by counting unit squares, write the area as length times width, and record it in square centimetres.
Students explain why a diagonal splits a rectangle into two congruent triangles and compute the area of each triangle as half of length times width.
Students find two rectangles where the one with the larger perimeter has the smaller area and explain why the boundary length cannot measure area.
Students design a pair of shapes other than rectangles in which the shape with the larger perimeter visibly has the smaller area.
Students find missing sides from areas, find path and tube areas by splitting into rectangles, and predict how area grows when every side of a square is doubled.

media.title: How do we find the area of a path around a park?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A path is laid around a rectangular park, and the park and the path together make a bigger rectangle. The area of the park is taken away from the area of the bigger rectangle, and the answer is checked by cutting the path into four strips.

media.title: How can a bent tube be straightened to find its area?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A spiral tube of the same width throughout is made of nine straight parts joined at bends. The lengths are added, the corner square shared at each bend is taken away once, and the tube is imagined straightened to find its area.

media.title: What happens to the areas when a square's side is doubled?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A square is divided into three regions, and then its side is doubled. A region with length x and width y becomes two x by two y, so its area is multiplied by four. A numbered check with a three by two region agrees.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: doubling every length multiplies each area by two times two, which is four, so each area grows by three times its old size. Watch for children who think doubling the side doubles the area.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text, opened only after the student tries the question

interaction_points.prompt: By how much does the area of each region increase?
interaction_points.answer: Each region becomes 4 times as big, an increase of 3 times its old area
covers: Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5)

source: Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5)
video_script.why: The child uses length times width to see that doubling every length multiplies every area by four.
video_script.substitution: Take a region with length x and width y, double both lengths, and compare the new area with the old area.
video_script.anchor: the square of the book that is divided into three regions
video_script.payoff_line: each region becomes four times as big

final_answer.value: Each region becomes 4 times as big, an increase of 3 times its old area
final_answer.spoken: four times as big, an increase of three times its old area

hold_back: an increase of 3 times its old area
never_show: the factor by which the areas grow, before the step that works it out
maths_rules: a region with length x and width y has area x × y
doubling the side of the square doubles every length in the figure, so the region becomes 2x by 2y
new area = 2x × 2y = 2 × 2 × x × y = 4xy, which is 4 times the old area xy
increase = 4xy − xy = 3xy, which is 3 times the old area

content.text:

content.text:
1. Predict first: in two identical rectangles, X is near a corner and Y is in the middle of the top. Which triangle on DC is bigger?
2. Drop the altitude from X to DC. It cuts the rectangle into two smaller rectangles, and each is halved by a side of the triangle.
3. So the triangle is half of the left rectangle plus half of the right one: half the whole, wherever X is.

content.text:
Worked example: X is on the top side of a rectangle with DC = 5 cm and height 4 cm. Find the area of ΔXDC.
1. Drop the altitude XY to DC. It splits the rectangle into two rectangles.
2. Each small rectangle is cut in half by XD or XC.
3. So ΔXDC is half of the whole rectangle: 1/2 × 5 × 4 = 10 cm².
Answer: 10 cm²

concepts.concept_name: Base and height: one half base times height

content.text:
To find the area of a triangle, what measurements do we need?
We need the sidelengths of the outer rectangle.
How do we get the outer rectangle from the given triangle?
BCDE is a rectangle (how?). Let us take its sidelengths to be height and base. Then, Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × base × height.
Since BXAE is a rectangle (how?), the height of the rectangle is the same as the height of the triangle.
Thus, if the height and the base of a triangle are known, we can find its area.
Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height.

concepts.concept_name: When the height falls outside the triangle

content.text:
Will this formula hold for the kind of triangle, around which we cannot draw a rectangle with BC as the base?
Here is one way to look at it. The area of ΔABC is the difference of the areas of ΔADC and ΔADB, each of which can be enclosed in a rectangle.
Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × h × DC − 1/2 × h × DB = 1/2 × h (DC − DB) = 1/2 × h × BC.
Thus, the area formula holds for all types of triangles.

content.text:
Worked example: In an obtuse triangle ABC the height from A meets CB extended at D, with h = 4 cm, DB = 3 cm and BC = 6 cm. Find the area.
1. DC = DB + BC = 3 + 6 = 9 cm.
2. Area of ΔADC = 1/2 × 4 × 9 = 18 cm². Area of ΔADB = 1/2 × 4 × 3 = 6 cm².
3. Area of ΔABC = 18 − 6 = 12 cm², and 1/2 × 4 × 6 = 12 cm² too.
Answer: 12 cm², the same as 1/2 × base × height

content.text:
Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height.
The height is perpendicular to the chosen base, even when it falls outside the triangle.
A rectangle and a triangle have equal areas when the triangle has twice the rectangle's height on the same base, or twice its base with the same height.

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 3): Find the area of ΔSUB, given that it is isosceles, SE is perpendicular to UB, and the area of ΔSEB is 24 sq. units.
1. In an isosceles triangle the perpendicular from S to UB meets it at its midpoint, so UE = EB.
2. ΔSUE and ΔSEB have the same base length and the same height SE, so equal areas.
3. Area of ΔSUB = 24 + 24 = 48 sq. units.
Answer: 48 sq. units

3. Join E to D. Triangle AED has base 2 × AB and height AD, so its area is 1/2 × 2AB × AD = AB × AD.
4. Another way: cut the rectangle along a diagonal and place the two halves side by side along the height to form one triangle.
Answer: A triangle on double the base with the same height (or double the height on the same base) has the rectangle's area

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 5): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a triangle into a rectangle of equal area.
1. Draw the height AX of triangle ABC on base BC.
2. Mark the midpoints of AB and AC and join them; this line is parallel to BC at half the height.
3. Drop perpendiculars from the two midpoints to BC. Cut off the two small top triangles and turn each into the gap below it.
4. The result is a rectangle with base BC and height 1/2 AX, so its area is 1/2 × BC × AX.
Answer: Cut along the line joining the midpoints of the two sides and swing the top pieces down: a rectangle on the same base with half the height

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students compare triangles drawn on the same side of identical rectangles, drop an altitude, and show each triangle is half the rectangle.
Students build the outer rectangle of a triangle from a line parallel to its base and two perpendiculars, and compute area as one half times base times height.
Students find the area of an obtuse triangle as the difference of two right triangles and show it still equals one half times base times height.
Students pick a base and its perpendicular height in triangles, find areas, and give methods to change a rectangle into a triangle and a triangle into a rectangle of equal area.

media.description: An isosceles triangle is split by a height into two triangles with equal bases and the same height. One of them has area twenty four square units, so the whole triangle has area forty eight square units.

triangles SUE and SEB have equal bases UE and EB and the same height SE, so equal areas: 1/2 × UE × SE = 1/2 × EB × SE = 24

check: folding along SE puts triangle SUE exactly on triangle SEB, so SUB is double SEB: 2 × 24 = 48

media.description: The Shulba Sutras ask for a method to change a rectangle into a triangle with the same area. Extend the bottom side by its own length and join the new end to the top corner, and the triangle on the double base has the rectangle's area.

media.description: The Shulba Sutras ask for a method to change a triangle into a rectangle with the same area. concepts.concept_name: Finding an altitude from the area

content.text:
Find BY.
BY can be found using the formula for the area of a triangle.
What is Area (ΔABC)?
Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × AX × BC = 15/2 sq. units.
The area of the triangle can also be written as Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × BY × AC = 1/2 × 4 × BY = 2 BY.
Thus, 2 BY = 15/2. So, BY = 15/4 = 3.75 units.

content.text:
Worked example: In ΔABC, AX = 3 is the height to BC = 5, and AC = 4. Find the height BY to AC.
1. Area = 1/2 × 3 × 5 = 7.5 square units.
2. Also, area = 1/2 × 4 × BY, which is 2 × BY.
3. So 2 × BY = 7.5, and BY = 7.5 ÷ 2 = 3.75 units.
Answer: BY = 3.75 units

concepts.concept_name: Diagonals and medians split area equally

content.text:
Are the 4 triangles obtained by drawing the diagonals of a rectangle (regions 1 to 4 in the figure) of equal areas?
Clearly, the triangles 1 to 4 are not four congruent triangles.
If OD and OB are taken as the bases, then we see that both triangles have the same altitude! We also have OB = OD, since the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other. So, the triangles 1 and 2 have equal areas.
In a triangle, the line joining a vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side divides the triangle into two triangles of equal areas.

content.text:
Worked example: The diagonals of an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle meet at O. Find the area of each of the four triangles.
1. The rectangle has area 8 × 6 = 48 cm².
2. Adjacent triangles have equal halves of a diagonal as bases and the same height, so equal areas.
3. All four are equal: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².
Answer: Each triangle is 12 cm², even though they are not congruent

2. Every triangle has base BC and the same height, the distance between the parallel lines.
3. So all the areas are equal: there is no largest or smallest. The perimeter does change: it keeps growing as the vertex slides far away, so there is no largest perimeter, but there is a smallest.

content.text:
Worked example: BC = 6 cm and line l is parallel to BC, 4 cm away. Find the area of a triangle on BC with its top on l, and say how it changes as the top moves.
1. Base = 6 cm, height = 4 cm for every position of the top.
2. Area = 1/2 × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².
3. Moving the top changes the slanting sides, not the height.
Answer: Always 12 cm²: equal areas; only the perimeter changes

content.text:
Intuition might suggest that the triangle with the minimum perimeter can be obtained by constructing the perpendicular bisector of BC. But how do we justify that this triangle has the least perimeter among all the triangles?
Let us imagine the line l as a mirror.
What can we say about the lengths of AB and its reflection AB′? Since ΔAXB ≅ ΔAXB′, AB = AB′.
So, finding point A that gives the shortest possible path B → A → C is the same as finding a point A that gives the shortest possible path B → A → C′. Choose A on the straight line BC′.
Analyse whether A lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

1. Predict first: is the top vertex for the shortest perimeter right above the middle of BC?
2. Reflect C in l to C′. Any path from A to C is as long as the path from A to C′.
3. The shortest way from B to C′ is a straight line. Where it crosses l is the best A, and by symmetry it is halfway along, on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

content.text:
Worked example: B and C are 3 cm below line l and BC = 8 cm. Find the smallest possible value of AB + AC with A on l.
1. Reflect C in l: C′ is 3 cm above l, so 6 cm above the line BC, directly over C.
2. BC′ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 6: √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10.
3. The straight line BC′ crosses l halfway across, above the midpoint of BC.
Answer: The smallest AB + AC is 10 cm, with A on the perpendicular bisector of BC

Figure it Out (triangles, question 2): Find the length of the altitude BY in ΔABC, where AX = 4 units is the height to BC = 6 units and AC = 8 units.

3. 4 × BY = 12, so BY = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 units.

Figure it Out (triangles, question 6): ABCD, BCEF and BFGH are identical squares, with H directly above B. The red region is the triangle DCH and the blue region is the part of square ABCD to the left of the line DH. (i) If the area of the red region is 49 sq. units, what is the area of the blue region? (ii) In another version, if the blue and red regions together are 180 sq. units, what is the area of each square?
1. Let each square have side s. Red: base DC = s, height CH = 2s, so area 1/2 × s × 2s, which is s².
2. DH rises 2s over a run of s, so it crosses AB at its midpoint: the blue triangle has legs s and s/2, area one quarter of s².
3. (i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units.
4. (ii) Blue + red is five quarters of s², so s² = 180 × 4 ÷ 5 = 144 sq. units.
Answer: (i) 12.25 sq. units (ii) 144 sq. units

3. 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Answer: ΔXMN is 1/4 of ΔXYZ

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 8): Gopal needs to carry water from the river to his water tank. He starts from his house. What is the shortest path from his house to the river and then to the water tank? Recreate the map and trace it.
1. Treat the river bank as a mirror line and reflect the water tank to the far side of it.
2. Join the house to the reflected tank with a straight line.
3. Where this line meets the river bank is the best point to fill water.
4. Walk house to that point, then to the real tank: this is as long as the straight line, the shortest possible.
Answer: Reflect the tank in the river bank; the straight line from the house to the reflection meets the bank at the best point

Neighbouring triangles share a height and have equal bases, so their areas match, and the rectangle's area is shared into four. Keeko doubts that the triangles on the long sides are bigger.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the diagonals of a rectangle cut it into four triangles of equal area, so each is a quarter of the rectangle. Watch for students who think the wider triangles must have more area.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

maths_rules: area of the rectangle = 8 × 6 = 48 cm²
OB = OD, because the diagonals of a rectangle cut each other in half
triangles AOB and AOD have bases OB and OD on the diagonal BD and the same height from A, so their areas are equal; the same holds for every pair of neighbours, so all four are equal
each triangle = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm²

the four triangles are not all congruent: two have base 8 and height 3, two have base 6 and height 4

media.title: What happens to the area as the top corner slides?
media.context: Area. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A base of six centimetres has a parallel line four centimetres above it, and a triangle stands on the base with its top corner on that line. The video finds the area from the base and the height, then slides the top corner and watches what stays and what changes. Keeko doubts that a leaning triangle with longer sides has more area.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: triangles on the same base with their top corner on a parallel line have the same height, so they have the same area. Watch for students who think longer sides mean more area.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

media.title: Where should A stand for the shortest path?
media.context: Area. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two corners sit three centimetres below a line, eight centimetres apart, and a third corner slides along the line. The video reflects one corner in the line, makes the path straight, and finds the smallest total length as ten centimetres. Keeko doubts that the spot straight above one corner is best.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: reflect one corner in the line, so the shortest path from B to the line to C becomes a straight line. Watch for students who pick the spot nearest to one corner.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: Where should A stand for the shortest path?
source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text
items: B and C are 3 cm below line l and BC = 8 cm. Find the smalle
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child sees that reflecting one corner in the line turns the bent path B to A to C into a straight path, so the shortest total is a straight line.

covers: B and C are 3 cm below line l and BC = 8 cm. Find the smalle

source: B and C are 3 cm below line l and BC = 8 cm. Find the smalle
video_script.why: The child sees that reflecting one corner in the line turns the bent path B to A to C into a straight path, so the shortest total is a straight line.
video_script.substitution: the book's reflection in the line l; B and C both 3 cm below l and BC = 8 cm
video_script.anchor: the book's line l as a mirror, with B and C below it and the corner A sliding along l
video_script.wrong_answer: the best spot is straight above B
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko puts A straight above B because that makes A B the shortest it can be. The total A B plus A C is what matters, and A C becomes very long.
video_script.payoff_line: The smallest total is ten centimetres

final_answer.spoken: ten centimetres

maths_rules: reflect C in the line l to get C'; C is 3 cm below l, so C' is 3 cm above l, which is 3 + 3 = 6 cm above C
for every A on l, AC = AC', so AB + AC = AB + AC'
the shortest path from B to C' is the straight line BC', so the smallest AB + AC is BC'
BC' is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs BC = 8 and CC' = 6: BC' = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 cm
the straight line BC' crosses l halfway up, directly above the midpoint of BC, so A is on the perpendicular bisector of BC
check: A straight above B gives AB = 3 and AC = √(64 + 9) = √73 (about 8.54), total about 11.54 cm, which is more than 10 cm
video_script.design: One line and two corners all video. The line is a mirror, one corner is reflected, and the bent path becomes a straight one. Keeko's doubt: stand nearest to one corner.

media.title: How long is the height B Y to the longer side?

media.description: A triangle has a base of six units, a height of four units to it, and another side of eight units. The area is found once, then written a second way with the long side as the base, and the two equal areas give the second height as three units.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: one triangle has one area, so half of one base times its height equals half of another base times its height. Watch for students who think every height of a triangle has the same length.

maths_rules: squares ABCD and BCEF sit side by side and BFGH sits on top of BCEF, so H is directly above B, a side length s above B

maths_rules: N is the midpoint of XZ, so XN = NZ; triangles XNY and NYZ have equal bases on XZ and the same height from Y, so they have equal areas
the two equal triangles fill ΔXYZ, so ΔXNY = 1/2 of ΔXYZ
M is the midpoint of XY, so XM = MY; triangles XMN and MYN have equal bases on XY and the same height from N, so they have equal areas
the two equal triangles fill ΔXNY, so ΔXMN = 1/2 of ΔXNY
ΔXMN = 1/2 × 1/2 of ΔXYZ = 1/4 of ΔXYZ
check: if ΔXYZ = 8, then ΔXNY = 4 and ΔXMN = 2, and 2 is 1/4 of 8

maths_rules: the river bank is a line l; the house H and the tank T are on the same side of it
reflect T in l to get T'; for every point P on l, PT = PT'

the shortest path from H to T' is the straight line HT', so the best P is where HT' meets l
any other P on l gives a bent path H to P to T', which is longer than the straight line HT'
the walk is H to P to T, as long as the straight line HT'

content.text:
Area of any Polygon
How do we find the area of this quadrilateral? What measurements do we need for this?
If we join BD, the quadrilateral ABCD gets divided into two triangles. By finding their areas, we can find the area of ABCD.
Can any polygon be divided into triangles?
It can be seen that any polygon can be divided into triangles. Thus, by knowing how to compute the area of a triangle, we can find the area of any polygon.
One can derive special formulae to find the areas of a parallelogram, rhombus and trapezium.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a quadrilateral has no single base and height. Which measurements would let us find its area?

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 1): Find the area of the quadrilateral ABCD given that AC = 22 cm, BM = 3 cm, DN = 3 cm, BM is perpendicular to AC, and DN is perpendicular to AC.

3. Shaded region = 180 − 30 − 40 = 110 cm².

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 3): What measurements would you need to find the area of a regular hexagon?
1. Join the centre to all six corners: six identical equilateral triangles.
2. Each triangle has a side of the hexagon as base and the distance from the centre to that side as height.
3. So the side length and the centre to side distance are enough: area = 6 × 1/2 × side × that distance.
Answer: The side length and the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 4): What fraction of the total area of the rectangle is the area of the blue region? (Two blue triangles stand on the top and bottom sides of the rectangle, with their tips meeting at a point inside.)
1. Each blue triangle has a full side of the rectangle as base: the length L.
2. Their heights, from the shared point to the top and to the bottom, add up to the width W.
3. Blue = 1/2 × L × h1 + 1/2 × L × h2 = 1/2 × L × (h1 + h2) = 1/2 × L × W.
Answer: Half of the rectangle is blue

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 5): Give a method to obtain a quadrilateral whose area is half that of a given quadrilateral.
1. Mark the midpoints of the four sides and join them in order.
2. Each corner triangle cut off is one quarter of the triangle made by a diagonal (both sides are halved).
3. The four corners together are one quarter of each pair of diagonal triangles, so half the quadrilateral; the inner quadrilateral is the other half.
Answer: Join the midpoints of the sides in order; the inner quadrilateral has half the area

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students cut a quadrilateral along a diagonal into two triangles, measure the height to the diagonal in each triangle, and add the two areas to get the polygon's area.
Students divide a pentagon into a rectangle and a triangle, or into triangles by diagonals from one corner, and add the pentagon's parts.
Students find polygon areas by splitting them into triangles, subtract corners from an enclosing rectangle, and reason about shaded fractions using equal bases and heights.

maths_rules: quadrilateral ABCD; P, Q, R, S are the midpoints of AB, BC, CD, DA
corner triangle APS has AP = 1/2 AB and AS = 1/2 AD at the same corner A, so its area is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 of triangle ABD
likewise triangle CQR = 1/4 of triangle CBD; so APS + CQR = 1/4 (ABD + CBD) = 1/4 of ABCD
with the diagonal AC: triangle BPQ = 1/4 of triangle BAC and triangle DRS = 1/4 of triangle DAC; so BPQ + DRS = 1/4 of ABCD
four corners = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 of ABCD; inner PQRS = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2 of ABCD

concepts.concept_name: Turn a parallelogram into a rectangle

content.text:
Parallelogram
Give a method to convert a parallelogram into a rectangle of equal area.
Construct AX perpendicular to CD. We call this a height of the parallelogram. Cut the parallelogram into ΔAXD and trapezium ABCX.
Can ΔAXD and ABCX fit together, as shown in the figure, to get a rectangle?
So, by the RHS congruency criterion, ΔBYC ≅ ΔAXD. Thus, ΔAXD will fit exactly over the region occupied by ΔBYC, and convert the parallelogram into a rectangle.
The process of cutting a figure into pieces and rearranging them to get a different figure of equal area is called dissection.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if we cut a parallelogram and move a piece, can it become a rectangle of the same area?
2. Cut along the height from one top corner. A right triangle comes away.
3. Slide it to the other end: it matches the gap exactly, because the two right triangles are congruent. Nothing is added or lost. This cut and rearrange is called dissection.

content.text:
Worked example: A parallelogram has base 9 cm and height 5 cm. Cut and slide it into a rectangle and find its area.
1. Cut along a height of 5 cm and slide the triangle across.
2. The rectangle is 9 cm long and 5 cm high.
3. Area = 9 × 5 = 45 cm².
Answer: 45 cm², the same as the parallelogram

concepts.concept_name: Base times height, with any base

content.text:
How do we find the area of a parallelogram by dissecting it into a rectangle?
Since DX = CY, we get DC = XY by adding the common part XC to DX and CY. Since DC is the base of the parallelogram, we get
Area of the parallelogram = base × height.
Can the area of the parallelogram be determined by taking another side as the base and its corresponding height?
Can the parallelogram be cut along CZ and rearranged to form a rectangle?
It can be seen that this is indeed possible, and so any side and its corresponding height can be used to find the area of a parallelogram.

content.text:
Worked example: A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 6 cm. The height on the 10 cm side is 4.8 cm. Find the area and the height on the 6 cm side.
1. Area = 10 × 4.8 = 48 cm².
2. With base 6 cm: 6 × height = 48.
3. Height = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm.
Answer: Area 48 cm²; the height on the 6 cm side is 8 cm

content.text:
Area of a parallelogram = base × height.
Any side can be the base, with the height perpendicular to it.
Same base and same height means the same area, whatever the slant.

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 1): Observe the parallelograms (a) to (g) drawn on a grid, all on equal bases between the same two grid lines. (i) What can we say about the areas of all these parallelograms? (ii) What can we say about their perimeters? Which figure appears to have the maximum perimeter, and which has the minimum perimeter?
1. (i) Each has the same base and the same height, so each has the same area, base × height.
2. (ii) The perimeter is twice the base plus twice the slanting side.
3. The more a parallelogram leans, the longer its slanting sides, so the larger its perimeter.
Answer: (i) All have equal areas. (ii) The perimeters differ: (g), leaning most, appears largest and (a), almost upright, smallest

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 2): Find the areas of the following parallelograms: (i) base 7 cm, height 4 cm, (ii) base 5 cm, height 3 cm, (iii) side 5 cm with height 4.8 cm drawn to it, (iv) side 2 cm with height 4.4 cm drawn to it.
1. (i) 7 × 4 = 28 cm².
2. (ii) 5 × 3 = 15 cm².
3. (iii) 5 × 4.8 = 24 cm².
4. (iv) 2 × 4.4 = 8.8 cm².
Answer: (i) 28 cm² (ii) 15 cm² (iii) 24 cm² (iv) 8.8 cm²

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 3): Find QN in parallelogram PQRS, where SR = 12 cm, the height QM to SR is 6 cm, PS = 7.6 cm, and QN is perpendicular to PS.
1. Area = SR × QM = 12 × 6 = 72 cm².
2. Also area = PS × QN = 7.6 × QN.
3. QN = 72 ÷ 7.6 ≈ 9.47 cm.
Answer: QN ≈ 9.47 cm

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 4): Consider a rectangle and a parallelogram of the same sidelengths: 5 cm and 4 cm. Which has the greater area? (Hint: imagine constructing them on the same base.)
1. Rectangle: 5 × 4 = 20 cm².
2. On the same 5 cm base, the parallelogram's height is shorter than its slanting 4 cm side.
3. So its area, 5 × height, is less than 20 cm².
Answer: The rectangle has the greater area

Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 5): Give a method to obtain a rectangle whose area is twice that of a given triangle. What are the different methods that you can think of?
1. Method 1: draw a line through the top vertex parallel to the base and perpendiculars to the base at its ends; the rectangle on the base and height is twice the triangle.
2. Method 2: take two copies of the triangle, join them into a parallelogram, then cut and slide it into a rectangle.
3. Either way the rectangle is base × height, twice 1/2 × base × height.
Answer: Build the rectangle on the base and height, or join two copies into a parallelogram and cut and slide

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 6): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to obtain a rectangle of the same area as a given triangle.
1. Join the midpoints of the two sides; this line is parallel to the base at half the height.
2. Drop perpendiculars from these midpoints to the base.
3. Cut off the two small top pieces and turn each down into the gap below it.
4. The result is a rectangle with the same base and half the height: 1/2 × base × height.
Answer: Cut at half the height and swing the top pieces down: a rectangle on the base with half the height

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 7): [Śulba-Sūtras] An isosceles triangle can be converted into a rectangle by dissection in a simpler way. Can you find out how to do it? (Hint: show that ΔADB and ΔADC can be made into halves of a rectangle.)
1. The altitude AD of isosceles ΔABC meets BC at its midpoint, giving two congruent right triangles.
2. Turn ΔADC over and place it against ΔADB with the hypotenuses together.
3. The two right triangles form a rectangle with sides BD and AD, area 1/2 × BC × AD.
Answer: Cut along the altitude and join the two right triangles along their slanting sides to make a rectangle BD by AD

Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 8): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to convert a rectangle into an isosceles triangle by dissection.
1. Cut the rectangle along a diagonal into two congruent right triangles.
2. Flip one triangle over and stand the two back to back, joined along the leg equal to the width.
3. They form an isosceles triangle with base twice the rectangle's length and height equal to its width.
Answer: Cut along a diagonal and stand the two right triangles back to back

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 9): Which has greater area: an equilateral triangle or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Which has greater area: two identical equilateral triangles together or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Give reasons.
1. Square of side s: area s × s.
2. The triangle's height is less than its slanting side s, so its area is less than 1/2 × s × s.
3. Two triangles make a rhombus with base s and height less than s, so less than s × s too.
Answer: The square is greater in both cases

media.title: What can we say about these leaning parallelograms?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Seven parallelograms stand on equal bases between the same two grid lines, some upright and some leaning far over. The board compares their areas by base and height, then compares their perimeters through the slanting sides, which grow as a shape leans.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the same base and the same height give the same area, but the perimeter changes with the slanting sides. Watch for students who think equal areas mean equal perimeters.

maths_rules: every parallelogram has the same base length b and the same height h, the distance between the two grid lines
area = base × height = b × h for every one, so all the areas are equal
perimeter = 2 × base + 2 × slanting side, and the base is the same for all
slanting side = square root of (h² + s²), where s is the sideways shift; it grows when s grows, so the more a shape leans the longer its perimeter
the most leaning shape has the longest perimeter and the least leaning the shortest; the book's figure was not in the text, so no letters are named

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students cut a right triangle off a parallelogram along a height, slide it to the other end, and use congruent triangles to show the rectangle formed has the same area.
Students apply parallelogram area as base times height, choose either side as base with its own perpendicular height, and find a missing height from the area.
Students compare parallelogram areas and perimeters on equal bases and heights, find areas and missing heights, and turn triangles and rectangles into each other by dissection.

maths_rules: rectangle with length l and width w; the diagonal makes two matching right triangles with legs l and w
a flipped copy joined along the legs of length w makes the two legs of length l lie in one straight line, since two right angles make a straight angle
the new triangle has base 2l and height w, and its two slanting sides are the diagonal, so it is isosceles
area = 1/2 × 2l × w = l × w, the area of the rectangle

concepts.concept_name: Dissect a rhombus into a rectangle

content.text:
Rhombus
Since a rhombus is a parallelogram, the area formula for a parallelogram holds for a rhombus as well. However, the additional properties of a rhombus give us another method to transform a rhombus into a rectangle of the same area by dissection. This method occurs in one of the Śulba-Sūtras.
Try working this out!
What are the sidelengths of the rectangle WXYZ?
XW = length of the diagonal AC, and WZ = half the length of the other diagonal BD.
Area of a rhombus = 1/2 × product of diagonals.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a rhombus has four equal sides and no right angles. Can its pieces make a rectangle?
2. The diagonals cross at right angles and halve each other, so they cut four right triangles.
3. Pair them into two small rectangles and stack them: one whole diagonal by half the other.

content.text:
Worked example: A rhombus has diagonals 12 cm and 8 cm. Dissect it into a rectangle and find the area.
1. The rectangle has one side 12 cm, the whole diagonal.
2. Its other side is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm, half the other.
3. Area = 12 × 4 = 48 cm².
Answer: 48 cm²

content.text:
Area of rhombus ABCD can also be determined by finding the areas of ΔADB and ΔCDB. What formula does this give us?
Since the diagonals are perpendicular to each other, we have Area (ΔADB) = 1/2 × AO × BD, and Area (ΔCDB) = 1/2 × CO × BD.
Simplify the expression to show that we get the same formula for the area of a rhombus in terms of its diagonals.

2. Cut along one diagonal. Each triangle has that diagonal as base and half the other diagonal as height.
3. Add the two: half of one diagonal times the other. The full product is the rectangle round the rhombus, twice too big.

content.text:
Worked example: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 6 cm. Find its area using two triangles.
1. Each triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.
2. Each triangle: 1/2 × 10 × 3 = 15 cm².
3. Rhombus: 15 + 15 = 30 cm², and 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².
Answer: 30 cm²

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 2): Give a method to convert a rectangle into a rhombus of equal area using dissection.
1. Cut the rectangle (length L, width W) into two halves, each L/2 long and W wide.
2. Cut each half along a diagonal: four congruent right triangles with legs L/2 and W.
3. Arrange them with the right angles meeting at one centre point: a rhombus with diagonals L and 2W.
4. Its area is 1/2 × L × 2W = L × W, the rectangle's area.
Answer: Cut into four congruent right triangles and put the right angles together at the centre

content.text:
Worked example: Trapezium ABCD on a grid has AB = 4 units, DC = 6 units and height AD = 4 units, with a right angle at D. Find its area.
1. Drop BM perpendicular to DC. ABMD is a 4 by 4 square: 16 square units.
2. ΔBMC has base MC = 6 − 4 = 2 and height 4: 1/2 × 2 × 4 = 4.
3. Area of ABCD = 16 + 4 = 20 square units.
Answer: 20 square units

content.text:
Consider a trapezium WXYZ with WX ∥ ZY. Find its area.
Construct WM ⊥ ZY, and XN ⊥ ZY (WM and XN perpendicular to ZY).
Is WXNM a rectangle?
Area WXYZ = Area (ΔWMZ) + Area WXNM + Area (ΔXNY).
Can the area of the trapezium be expressed in terms of a, b and h?
Area of a trapezium = 1/2 × height × sum of the parallel sides.

content.text:
Worked example: Trapezium WXYZ has WX = 5 units, ZY = 9 units and height 4 units, with ZM = 2 and NY = 2. Find its area.
1. Rectangle WXNM: 5 × 4 = 20.
2. Each end triangle: 1/2 × 2 × 4 = 4.
3. Total = 4 + 20 + 4 = 28, and 1/2 × 4 × (5 + 9) = 28.
Answer: 28 square units

Worked example: A slanting trapezium has parallel sides AB = 6 cm and DC = 10 cm and height 5 cm. Use Approach 2 to find its area.
1. Parallelogram ABGD: 6 × 5 = 30 cm².
2. Triangle BGC has base 10 − 6 = 4 cm: 1/2 × 4 × 5 = 10 cm².
3. Total = 30 + 10 = 40 cm², and 1/2 × 5 × (6 + 10) = 40 cm².
Answer: 40 cm²

content.text:
Finding the Area Using Two Copies of the Trapezium
Consider two copies of the given trapezium in which AB ∥ CD. Rotate the second copy as shown.
What figure will we get when the two trapeziums are joined along BC?
Since AB ∥ CD, we have x + y = 180, since they are internal angles along the same side of the transversal (BC). Therefore, the resulting figure is a quadrilateral.
What type of a quadrilateral is this?
Area of the trapezium = 1/2 × Area of the parallelogram = 1/2 h(a + b).

1. Predict first: two copies of a trapezium, one turned round, joined along a slanting side. What shape?
2. The angles at the joint add to 180, so the edges run straight: the short side of one continues the long side of the other, making a side a + b long.
3. Opposite sides are parallel: a parallelogram of area (a + b) × h, and the trapezium is half of it.

Worked example: A trapezium has parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm and height 6 cm. Use two copies to find its area.
1. The parallelogram has base 7 + 11 = 18 cm and height 6 cm.
2. Its area is 18 × 6 = 108 cm².
3. The trapezium is half: 108 ÷ 2 = 54 cm².
Answer: 54 cm²

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 3): Find the areas of the following figures: (i) a trapezium with parallel sides 10 ft and 7 ft and height 16 ft between them, (ii) parallel sides 24 m and 36 m, height 14 m, (iii) parallel sides 14 in and 6 in, height 10 in, (iv) parallel sides 12 ft and 18 ft, height 8 ft.
1. (i) 1/2 × 16 × (10 + 7) = 1/2 × 16 × 17 = 136 ft².
2. (ii) 1/2 × 14 × (24 + 36) = 1/2 × 14 × 60 = 420 m².
3. (iii) 1/2 × 10 × (14 + 6) = 1/2 × 10 × 20 = 100 in².
4. (iv) 1/2 × 8 × (12 + 18) = 1/2 × 8 × 30 = 120 ft².
Answer: (i) 136 ft² (ii) 420 m² (iii) 100 in² (iv) 120 ft²

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 4): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to convert an isosceles trapezium to a rectangle using dissection.
1. Mark the midpoint of each slanting side.
2. Through each midpoint draw a line perpendicular to the parallel sides.
3. Cut off the small corner triangle below each midpoint and turn it about the midpoint into the gap above it; the two halves of each slanting side match.
4. The result is a rectangle with height h and length 1/2 × (a + b).
Answer: Cut through the midpoints of the slanting sides at right angles to the base and swing the corner pieces up: a rectangle 1/2 × (a + b) by h

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 5): Here is one of the ways to convert trapezium ABCD into a rectangle EFGH of equal area. Given the trapezium ABCD, how do we find the vertices of the rectangle EFGH? (Hint: if ΔAHI ≅ ΔDGI and ΔBEJ ≅ ΔCFJ, then the trapezium and rectangle have equal areas.)
1. Mark I and J, the midpoints of the slanting sides AD and BC.
2. Through I draw the line perpendicular to DC; it meets DC at G and the line AB extended at H.
3. Through J do the same to get F on DC and E on AB extended.
4. Since AI = DI and the angles match, ΔAHI ≅ ΔDGI and ΔBEJ ≅ ΔCFJ, so EFGH has the trapezium's area.
Answer: Take the midpoints I and J of the slanting sides and draw perpendiculars to DC through them; they meet DC and line AB at G, H, F and E

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 6): Using the idea of converting a trapezium into a rectangle of equal area, and vice versa, construct a trapezium of area 144 cm².
1. A trapezium has the area of a rectangle with sides h and 1/2 × (a + b).
2. Choose a 12 cm by 12 cm rectangle: area 144 cm². So h = 12 and a + b = 24.
3. Take a = 8 and b = 16: 1/2 × 12 × (8 + 16) = 144.
Answer: For example, parallel sides 8 cm and 16 cm with height 12 cm (any a + b and h with h × (a + b) = 288 works)

Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 7): A regular hexagon is divided into a trapezium, an equilateral triangle, and a rhombus, as shown. Find the ratio of their areas.
1. Joining the centre to the corners splits a regular hexagon into 6 equal equilateral triangles.
2. The trapezium is half the hexagon: 3 of these triangles.
3. The rhombus is 2 of them and the equilateral triangle is 1.
Answer: Trapezium : triangle : rhombus = 3 : 1 : 2

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 8): ZYXW is a trapezium with ZY ∥ WX. A is the midpoint of XY. Show that the area of the trapezium ZYXW is equal to the area of ΔZWB, where ZA extended meets WX extended at B.
1. YA = XA, since A is the midpoint of XY.
2. ∠ZAY = ∠BAX (vertically opposite) and ∠ZYA = ∠BXA (alternate angles, since ZY ∥ WB).
3. So ΔZYA ≅ ΔBXA (ASA): they have equal areas.
4. Trapezium ZYXW = ZAXW + ΔZYA = ZAXW + ΔBXA = ΔZWB.
Answer: ΔZYA ≅ ΔBXA, so swapping one for the other shows the trapezium and ΔZWB have equal areas
content.publication_text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 8): ZYXW is a trapezium with ZY ∥ WX. A is the midpoint of XY. Show that the area of the trapezium ZYXW is equal to the area of ΔZWB, where ZA extended meets WX extended at B.
1. YA = XA, since A is the midpoint of XY.
2. ∠ZAY = ∠BAX (vertically opposite) and ∠ZYA = ∠BXA (alternate angles, since ZY ∥ WB).
3. So ΔZYA ≅ ΔBXA (ASA): they have equal areas.
4. Trapezium ZYXW = ZAXW + ΔZYA = ZAXW + ΔBXA = ΔZWB.
Answer: ΔZYA ≅ ΔBXA, so swapping one for the other shows the trapezium and ΔZWB have equal areas

media.title: Does the area rule still work for a trapezium that leans?
media.context: Area. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A trapezium leans to one side, so a line cannot simply drop straight down from each top corner. media.title: How can two copies of a trapezium give its area?
media.context: Area. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two copies of a trapezium are joined along a slanting side, and they fit into one parallelogram. Its base is the two parallel sides side by side, so its area is that base times the height, and the trapezium is half of it. Keeko doubts that the joined copies make a parallelogram and wonders if they make a six sided figure.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: two copies of a trapezium make a parallelogram whose base is the sum of the parallel sides, so the trapezium is half of it. Watch for students who give the area of the parallelogram as the area of the trapezium.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

video_script.why: The child knows the area of a parallelogram and here sees why the trapezium is half of the two parallel sides added, times the height.

video_script.anchor: two copies of the trapezium, one turned half way round and joined to the other along a slanting side
video_script.wrong_answer: six sided figure
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks the two joined copies make a six sided figure, because each copy has a slanting side that could bend at the join. The two angles along the joined side add up to a straight angle, so the edges run straight and the shape has four sides.
video_script.payoff_line: The trapezium covers fifty four square centimetres.

final_answer.spoken: fifty four square centimetres

maths_rules: trapezium: parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm, height 6 cm
two copies joined along a slanting side make a parallelogram with base 7 + 11 = 18 cm and height 6 cm
parallelogram area = 18 x 6 = 108 cm2
trapezium = half of the parallelogram: 108 / 2 = 54 cm2
the two angles along the joined side add up to 180, so the joined edges are straight and the shape has four sides

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students find the area of a trapezium on a grid by breaking it into a rectangle and right triangles and counting the square units in each trapezium part.
Students cut a trapezium by two heights into a rectangle and two triangles, add the areas, and reach one half the height times the sum of the parallel sides.
Students handle a trapezium whose height falls outside the longer side by adding and subtracting triangles, and check that the trapezium formula still holds.
Students join two copies of a trapezium into a parallelogram with base equal to the sum of the parallel sides and halve its area to get the trapezium's area.
Students find trapezium areas from parallel sides and height, convert trapeziums into rectangles and triangles by dissection, and compare the parts of a dissected hexagon.

media.description: An isosceles trapezium is cut at the midpoints of its slanting sides, and the two corner pieces turn half way round into the gaps above them. The pieces make a rectangle of the same area, as tall as the trapezium and as long as half the sum of the parallel sides.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: cut at the midpoints of the slanting sides and turn each corner piece about its midpoint. Watch for students who cut anywhere along the slanting side, because then the pieces do not fit.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

maths_rules: isosceles trapezium: slanting sides equal, top side a, bottom side b, height h
mark the midpoint of each slanting side
through each midpoint draw the line at right angles to the parallel sides
each line cuts off a small corner triangle below the midpoint; it is congruent to the gap triangle above the midpoint (equal angles at the midpoint, right angles, equal halves of the slanting side)
turn each corner triangle half way round about its midpoint into the gap above it
the result is a rectangle of height h and length 1/2 x (a + b), with the same area as the trapezium

media.title: How do we find the corners of the equal rectangle?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A trapezium ABCD is turned into a rectangle EFGH of the same area. The corners come from the midpoints of the two slanting sides: lines at right angles to the bottom side through the midpoints meet the bottom side and the top side extended, and each corner triangle matches the gap above it.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: find the midpoints of the slanting sides, draw lines at right angles to the bottom side through them, and the four meeting points are the corners. Watch for students who draw the lines from the corners of the trapezium instead of from the midpoints.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

maths_rules: trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to DC
I is the midpoint of AD and J is the midpoint of BC
the line through I at right angles to DC meets DC at G and the line AB extended at H
the line through J at right angles to DC meets DC at F and the line AB extended at E
AI = DI, the angles at H and G are right angles and the angles at I are vertically opposite, so triangle AHI and triangle DGI match
in the same way triangle BEJ and triangle CFJ match, so rectangle EFGH has the area of the trapezium

media.title: How do we draw a trapezium with a chosen area?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A trapezium has the same area as a rectangle as tall as the trapezium and as long as half the sum of its parallel sides. So we choose a rectangle of area one hundred forty four square centimetres, read off the height and the sum of the parallel sides, and pick two sides that add up to it.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a trapezium has the area of a rectangle of the same height and half the sum of the parallel sides, so we can work backwards from a chosen rectangle. Watch for students who think only one trapezium can have the given area.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

maths_rules: area of a trapezium = 1/2 x h x (a + b) = h x (1/2 x (a + b)), the area of a rectangle with sides h and 1/2 x (a + b)
choose a rectangle of area 144: 12 x 12 = 144, so h = 12 and 1/2 x (a + b) = 12, so a + b = 24
choose a = 8, then b = 24 - 8 = 16
any h and a + b with h x (a + b) = 288 works

media.title: What is the ratio of the three parts of a hexagon?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A regular hexagon is cut from its centre into six equal triangles. The trapezium holds three of them, the rhombus two and the triangle one, so the three areas are in the ratio three to one to two, and together they make six.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: join the centre of a regular hexagon to its corners to get six equal triangles, then count the triangles in each part. Watch for students who say three parts must be in the ratio one to one to one.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

maths_rules: joining the centre of a regular hexagon to its six corners gives 6 equal equilateral triangles
the trapezium is half the hexagon: 3 of these triangles

ratio trapezium : triangle : rhombus = 3 : 1 : 2

concepts.concept_name: The area of an A4 sheet and a tabletop

content.text:
Areas in Real Life
What do you think is the area of an A4 sheet? Its sidelengths are 21 cm and 29.7 cm. Now find its area.
What do you think is the area of the tabletop that you use at school or at home? You could perhaps try to visualise how many A4 sheets can fit on your table.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the area of an A4 sheet, then estimate a table that is covered by 3 rows of 4 sheets.
1. A4 sheet: 21 × 29.7 = 623.7 cm².
2. The table holds 3 × 4 = 12 sheets.
3. Table ≈ 12 × 623.7 = 7484.4 cm², about 7500 cm².
Answer: The sheet is 623.7 cm²; the table is about 7500 cm²

content.text:
What do you think is the area of your classroom? Areas of classroom, house, etc., are generally measured in ft² or m².
What do you think is the area of your school? Make an estimate and compare it with the actual data.
Larger areas of land are also measured in acres. 1 acre = 43560 ft².
Besides these units, different parts of India use different local units for measuring area, such as bigha, gaj, katha, dhur, cent, ankanam, etc.
Find out the local unit of area measurement in your region.

content.text:
Worked example: A classroom is 8 m by 6 m. How many such classrooms would fit in 1 km²?
1. Classroom: 8 × 6 = 48 m².
2. 1 km² = 1000 × 1000 = 1000000 m².
3. 1000000 ÷ 48 ≈ 20833 classrooms.
Answer: About 20833 classrooms

content.text:

content.text:

3. Check: 25 × 6.4516 = 161.29.
Answer: 161.29 cm² = 25 in²

content.text:
In-text question (areas in real life, question 3): How many times is your village/town/city bigger than your school?
1. Write both areas in the same unit, for example m².
2. For a school ground 100 m by 80 m: 100 × 80 = 8000 m². For a town of 10 km²: 10 × 1000000 = 10000000 m².
3. Divide: 10000000 ÷ 8000 = 1250.
Answer: For a 10 km² town and an 8000 m² school, 1250 times; use your own town and school data

tool_config.title: Square Unit Scaler: Side and Area
tool_config.idea: When one unit is k times as long as another, a square of the larger unit holds k × k squares of the smaller, so a square unit converts by the length factor multiplied by itself: 1 square foot is 12 × 12 = 144 square inches, and 1 square inch is 2.54 × 2.54 = 6.4516 square centimetres (a factor that is not whole leaves partial squares and strips in the tiling).
tool_config.screen: A unit square that can be tiled by smaller squares, a unit pair chosen from metre and centimetre, foot and inch, inch and centimetre, kilometre and metre, a live readout of the length factor and the area factor, and a converter row that turns a given area from one unit to the other.
student_does: Predict the area factor before the square is tiled.
Choose a unit pair and watch the side split into equal parts.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students compute the area of an A4 sheet from its side lengths and estimate a tabletop's area by counting how many sheets cover it.
Students convert lengths between inches and centimetres, then show that one square inch equals 2.54 × 2.54 square centimetres and convert square units both ways.
Students choose square metres, acres or square kilometres for rooms, schools and towns, find how many square metres make a square kilometre, and meet local area units.
Students convert between square centimetres, square inches and square feet, compare the sizes of a town and a school, and plan how to find the largest and smallest cities.

content.text:
Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height.
The area of any polygon can be evaluated by breaking it into triangles.
Area of a parallelogram = base × height.
Area of a rhombus = 1/2 × product of its diagonals.
Area of a trapezium = 1/2 × height × sum of parallel sides.

content.text:
1. Our opening puzzle is settled: a square can be cut into four equal areas in endless ways, because area counts squares, not shapes.
2. A triangle is half a rectangle; any polygon is a set of triangles; a parallelogram slides into a rectangle; a rhombus is half the rectangle on its diagonals; two trapeziums make a parallelogram.
3. Every height is perpendicular to its base. Still open for you: estimate the area of your town.
